paragraphs: The services shown above take enquiries from people in Edinburgh, among them the City of Edinburgh Council's own service, Foster with Edinburgh, and independent agencies that work across Scotland. The council's fostering team runs a training calendar and support groups for the carers it approves.

For 2026-27 the council changed how it pays its own carers. Its budget agreed a single fee that no longer depends on the age of the child, with higher specialist fees, including for caring for a disabled child, and the age-related Scottish Recommended Allowance, which covers a child's day-to-day costs, is paid on top. Announcing the change in May 2026, the council said people thinking about fostering can hold back because they worry about the effect on their household's finances, and that it wanted to encourage them. We do not yet have an Edinburgh pay page, so check the current figures with the council.

Edinburgh has also appealed for particular kinds of carer. In April 2023 it began looking for host family carers for unaccompanied young people aged 16 and over who had come to the city fleeing war and persecution, and for carers for children and young people from minority ethnic backgrounds. It asked for a spare room, time, patience and commitment, and the ability to take part in meetings in English, and said host family carers could keep working.

Across Scotland you can apply through your local council, an independent agency or a charity. You need to live in the UK full time and be 18 or over, though some services will not approve anyone under 21, and there is no upper age limit. A spare bedroom is usually expected. Renting, working full time and having children of your own do not rule you out, although some councils limit the kinds of fostering open to people in full-time work. The assessment, with home visits, preparation groups, checks and references, can take 6 to 12 months and ends at a fostering panel; your approval is reviewed after a year and then every two years.

Fostering with the council means caring for Edinburgh's own children with its team behind you; an agency approves, trains and supports you itself, and councils, Edinburgh among them, ask it to care for children who need a home. Ask the council and two or three of the services above which children most need homes, what training they offer and what help there is out of hours. If you live outside the city, see our pages for West Lothian, East Lothian, Fife and Scotland.
